title: Passing Data by Pointer or Reference
learningObjectives: Choose pointer, reference or value parameter forms.
Use pointer parameters for optional inputs when appropriate.
Use references for required objects and mutation.
Use const references for read-only large inputs.
Prefer value return for simple results and avoid dangling aliases.

understand.concept: Pointer parameters can express optional data or modify caller objects; reference parameters express required aliases. Value parameters copy objects.
understand.whyItMatters: Choosing parameter style clarifies function contracts and copying costs.
understand.explain: Use const reference for read-only large objects; use reference for intentional mutation; pointer when nullable/indirection is meaningful.

examples.title: Optional pointer parameter
examples.explanation: Pointer parameter communicates that null may be supplied.

examples.title: Required reference
examples.explanation: Reference parameter requires a valid object and modifies it.

examples.title: Return value avoids alias
examples.explanation: A value return avoids a lifetime-sensitive reference.

examples.title: Choose parameter style
examples.explanation: Pointer version can represent absence; reference version requires an object.

practise.guidedTask: For Passing Data by Pointer or Reference, draw the object and pointer/reference relationships for every example. Mark owner, target, constness, lifetime, validity of access, and any operation that could invalidate the pointer or reference.
practise.independentTask: Write a focused C++ exercise for Passing Data by Pointer or Reference. Demonstrate at least three cases, including a safe usage and a boundary/invalid case explained in comments but not executed. State who owns the resource and when each object/view is valid.
hints: Draw the pointer/reference and its target object.
Mark whether the object is alive and who owns it.
Check nullptr and bounds before access.
Consider invalidation, deletion and scope exit.
Use standard containers or smart pointers when they express ownership more safely.

questions.explanation: Reference requires an object to bind to.
const reference avoids copies and mutation.
Returning by value avoids aliasing local storage.
